in_text_mentions: d vessels, especially the inner arterial wall (intima). Although the pathogenesis is not fully understood, initial loss of vascular immune tolerance triggers an aberrant cascade of disease processes involving both the innate and adaptive immune systems. The disease progresses from early granulomatous inflammation to a chronic inflammatory reaction that results in smooth muscle proliferation into the vascular intima and fibrosis in the tunica adventitia with eventual vascular narrowing. The consequences of this inflammatory damage include stenosis (Figure 1), thrombosis, and aneurysm formation.

in_text_mentions: nches; collateral vessels are indicative of the chronicity of stenotic lesions (99, 102, 103). On the other hand, CTA has a better resolution—and it provides excellent anatomic detail in 3D reconstruction images (Figure 5)—, but exposes the patient to high radiation and it is not suit for repeat follow-up assessments. It is certainly helpful when MRA is not available. The lower thoracic and abdominal aorta is narrow and irregular down to the aortic bifurcation (star).

panels.figure_caption: Typical “macaroni sign” in a TAK patient. (a) The B‐mode ultrasound image shows the right common carotid artery in a 39‐year‐old woman diagnosed with type IIa TAK. (b) A transverse scan of the same vessel shows a marked, concentric, hypoechoic wall thickening that reduces the lumen by 35%.

in_text_mentions: ntext of systemic inflammation. Brain imaging confirmed an ischemic stroke in the right middle cerebral artery territory. CT angiography and MR angiography demonstrated multiple arterial lesions involving the carotid arteries (Figures 1, 2). Doppler ultrasound of the supra-aortic vessels showed circumferential hypoechoic wall thickening of the carotid arteries (“macaroni sign”), consistent with inflammatory involvement (Figure 3). High-dose corticosteroid therapy (1 mg/kg/day) was initiated, along with antiplatelet therapy. The clinical course was favorable, with partial neurological recovery.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Coronal fused PET/MR and whole-body MIP demonstrate metabolically active large-vessel inflammation (FDG uptake) in the ascending aorta and common carotid arteries in a child with Takayasu arteritis. B: Axial T2-weighted MR and fused PET/MR show FDG-avid circumferential wall thickening of the abdominal aorta without significant stenosis in a child with Takayasu arteritis. C: Axial MR and fused PET/MR with whole-body MIP demonstrate subtle FDG uptake in the aortic arch wall in a child with Takayasu arteritis.
panels.attribution_text: Kumar et al. FDG-PET/MR in paediatric pyrexia of unknown origin: early detection of Takayasu arteritis—a single-centre experience. Frontiers in pediatrics None. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Representative de-identified 18F-FDG-PET/MR studies demonstrate metabolically active large-vessel inflammation in children with pre-stenotic Takayasu arteritis presenting with pyrexia of unknown origin. (A) Coronal fused 18F-FDG-PET/MR (upper) with the corresponding whole-body PET maximum-intensity projection (MIP; lower) shows diffuse FDG-avid wall uptake along the ascending aorta and both common carotid arteries (arrows). (B) Axial T2-weighted MR (left) and the corresponding fused axial PET/MR (right) at the level of the upper abdomen in another patient show FDG-avid circumferential wall thickening of the abdominal aorta (arrow). (C) Axial MR and fused axial PET/MR (upper) with whole-body PET MIPs (lower) show subtle FDG uptake within the wall of the aortic arch (arrow). In each patient, arterial wall FDG uptake equal to or exceeding hepatic background was taken to indicate active large-vessel vasculitis; all studies were performed before glucocorticoid initiation, and no haemodynamically significant luminal stenosis was present at baseline.
in_text_mentions: ies involved in individual patients included the common and internal carotid arteries; the brachiocephalic trunk; the celiac artery; and the iliofemoral, axillary, and popliteal vessels (Figure 1). Uptake ranged from subtle focal to diffuse circumferential wall involvement, with the SUVmax in the most active segment ranging from 2.7 to 7.4 (median 4.8). On the co-registered MR angiographic component, mural thickening was evident, but there was no haemodynamically significant (>50%) luminal stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysm in any patient at baseline; a representative study is shown in Figure 2.

in_text_mentions: To further assess the degree and distribution of arterial stenoses, numerous Doppler ultrasound scans were performed. Carotid Dopplers revealed high-grade stenoses at the bifurcation of the left common carotid artery (Figure 1(a)) and medium grade at the bifurcation of the right common carotid artery. Further assessment demonstrated significant wall thickening in both subclavian arteries, with diminished flow on the left.

Given these findings, MR angiography of the head, neck, and thorax (Figure 1(b)) was performed, revealing both acute inflammation and extensive established disease: complete occlusion of the left subclavian and both axillary arteries with good collateralisation. Numerous short high-grade stenoses of the left common carotid artery with complete occlusion of the ipsilateral external carotid artery were seen. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: MRA image demonstrating right renal artery stenosis, a classic manifestation of Takayasu arteritis. b: MRA image of the great vessels demonstrating multiple arterial stenoses and occlusions consistent with Takayasu arteritis. c: MRA image showing dilated ascending aorta with associated severe aortic regurgitation in a young female patient with Takayasu arteritis. d: MRA image demonstrating subclavian artery stenosis with collateral formation in Takayasu arteritis.
panels.attribution_text: Perera et al. Takayasu arteritis: criteria for surgical intervention should not be ignored.. International journal of vascular medicine 2013. doi:10.1155/2013/618910. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Indications for surgical intervention in Takayasu arteritis. Surgery should not be undertaken lightly in patients with TA. However, the outcome of intervention in those with serious complications is good and improved if disease activity can be controlled prior to surgery. The figure shows MRA studies. (a) A right renal artery stenosis subsequently successfully treated by percutaneous angioplasty with resolution of hypertension. (b) Severe disease of the great vessels including stenoses of the right subclavian and common carotid arteries (arrows) and occlusion of the left subclavian and left common carotid arteries (stars). The patient suffered severe cerebrovascular symptoms and underwent successful bypass surgery. (c) A dilated ascending aorta with associated severe aortic regurgitation in a young female patient who required aortic valve replacement. (d) Although patients commonly suffer claudication symptoms as a consequence of subclavian artery stenosis (arrow), these often improve following the development of collaterals (stars) as shown here, precluding the need for intervention.
in_text_mentions: ize. The published literature however indicates that these procedures should be carefully considered and that restenosis is common; therefore intervention should be reserved for specific indications (Figure 3) [3, 8, 15, 23]. Rates of surgical intervention vary between centres from 12% to 70%, but it seems likely that less than 20% of patients with TA actually require revascularization [9, 15, 39]. source_variant.figure_caption: Indications for surgical intervention in Takayasu arteritis. Surgery should not be undertaken lightly in patients with TA. However, the outcome of intervention in those with serious complications is good and improved if disease activity can be controlled prior to surgery. The figure shows MRA studies. (a) A right renal artery stenosis subsequently successfully treated by percutaneous angioplasty with resolution of hypertension. (b) Severe disease of the great vessels including stenoses of the right subclavian and common carotid arteries (arrows) and occlusion of the left subclavian and left common carotid arteries (stars). The patient suffered severe cerebrovascular symptoms and underwent successful bypass surgery. (c) A dilated ascending aorta with associated severe aortic regurgitation in a young female patient who required aortic valve replacement. (d) Although patients commonly suffer claudication symptoms as a consequence of subclavian artery stenosis (arrow), these often improve following the development of collaterals (stars) as shown here, precluding the need for intervention.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Coronal contrast-enhanced CT showing abrupt truncation of supra-aortic vessels consistent with branch artery occlusion in Takayasu arteritis. B: Sagittal CT reconstruction showing concentric inflammatory wall thickening of the aorta and cervical arteries, a classic finding of Takayasu arteritis. C: Coronal CT with measurements demonstrating mural thickening and near-complete occlusion of supra-aortic branch vessels, consistent with Takayasu arteritis.
panels.attribution_text: Ferrufino Mejia et al. Severe Pediatric Takayasu Arteritis Presenting With Cerebral Ischemia and Supra-Aortic Trunk Occlusion.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.96917. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showing wall thickening and the truncation of supra-aortic vessels (A) Coronal view showing the abrupt truncation of the great vessels with loss of opacification beyond the aortic arch. (B) Sagittal reconstruction revealing the concentric inflammatory wall thickening of the ascending aorta and cervical arteries. (C) Coronal view with multiplanar measurements confirming the mural thickening and near-complete occlusion of the brachiocephalic trunk and left common carotid artery (orange circle).
in_text_mentions: These findings correlated with contrast-enhanced CT angiography, which showed circumferential wall thickening and abrupt truncation of the great vessels beyond the aortic arch (Figure 3A-3C) and explained the previously reported absence of luminal opacification, reflecting complete hemodynamic occlusion rather than isolated mural thickening.

in_text_mentions: Carotid ultrasonography revealed the macaroni sign in the common carotid artery (Figure 1, A). Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging showed circumferential wall thickening of the aorta and the 3 branch vessels of the aortic arch (Figure 1, B). Additional imaging findings on contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) included dilatation of the ascending aorta (maximum diameter: 43 mm; Figure 1, C) and main pulmonary artery (maximum diameter: 47 mm; Figure 1). Preoperative CT showed an annular diameter of 28 mm, a sinus of Valsalva diameter of 39 mm, and a sinotubular junction diameter of

Laboratory tests on admission showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (104 mm/h), whereas positron emission tomography−CT demonstrated mild radiotracer uptake in the aorta and cervical branch vessels (Figure 1, D), suggesting high disease activity. To minimize the risk of postoperative anastomotic pseudoaneurysm or prosthetic valve dehiscence, surgical intervention was deferred until inflammatory marker normalization.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Gross photograph demonstrating fusiform aneurysms of the aorta and iliac arteries, a known complication of Takayasu arteritis. B: Histology section (40x) showing focal intimal thickening, consistent with the inflammatory process of Takayasu arteritis described in the text. C: Histology section (200x) showing transmural lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, confirming granulomatous panarteritis. D: Elastic stain showing disruption of the elastic lamina, a characteristic feature of Takayasu arteritis. E: Gross photograph of brain showing saccular aneurysms in the context of Takayasu arteritis, as described in the case report.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Coronal CT angiographic image from a patient with Takayasu arteritis demonstrates diffuse circumferential aortic mural thickening, a characteristic large-vessel manifestation. b: The 3D CT angiographic reconstruction visibly shows multifocal aortic dilatation and aneurysmal outpouchings in the disease-focused evaluation of Takayasu arteritis. c: The axial CT angiographic image and red arrows identify bilateral thin-caliber renal arteries, indicating renal arterial narrowing in this Takayasu arteritis angiogram. The caption does not establish the specific tapered morphology required for the supplied stenosis finding key. d: The coronal CT image with white arrows demonstrates bilateral small kidneys, consistent with renal atrophy in the reported renal-artery involvement and chronic kidney disease presentation of Takayasu arteritis.

C: Axial CTA at the aortic arch level showing circumferential wall thickening and an occluded aorto-carotid bypass graft. D: Axial CTA demonstrating thickened aortic wall (thick arrow) at the level of the aortic arch and descending aorta.

findings.evidence: long-segment stenosis of the right vertebral artery involving the V3 and V4 segments

panels.rationale: Single-image MR angiography from Takayasu arteritis case series showing long-segment stenosis of right vertebral artery V3-V4, explicitly attributed to Takayasu arteritis in caption and in-text mention, matching smooth tapered arterial stenosis vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Said IsmaIl et al. Severe Neurovascular and Cardiovascular Manifestations of Takayasu Arteritis: A Case Series and Review of the Literature.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.108590. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 11.
panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance angiography demonstrating a long-segment stenosis of the right vertebral artery involving the V3 and V4 segments. This diffuse luminal narrowing is consistent with inflammatory involvement of large vessels in Takayasu arteritis. 1: right vertebral artery; 2: left vertebral artery
in_text_mentions: with active inflammation (Figure 10). MR angiography suggested diffuse involvement of the aorta and its major branches, with predominant involvement of the right vertebral artery. In particular, a long-segment stenosis of the right vertebral artery involving the V3 and V4 segments was identified, consistent with inflammatory large-vessel vasculitis (Figure 11). There was no evidence of infective endocarditis, based on the absence of valvular vegetations on echocardiography, negative blood cultures, absence of an infectious syndrome, and favorable clinical evolution without antibiotic therapy.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Coronal PET in 45-year-old female diagnosed Takayasu arteritis showing grade 3 FDG uptake at supra-aortic origins. B: T2-weighted MRI showing arterial wall thickening at site of FDG uptake in Takayasu arteritis case. C: Post-contrast T1-weighted image showing wall enhancement/thickened wall at supra-aortic origins in Takayasu arteritis. D: Fusion MR angiography/PET showing co-registered FDG uptake at inflamed supra-aortic vessel wall in Takayasu arteritis. E: Fusion PET/T2-weighted image showing FDG uptake co-registered to thickened arterial wall in Takayasu arteritis.

panels.figure_caption: Case of Takayasu arteritis (TA) in a 45-year-old female with arthralgia, vascular claudication, and acute phase reactants refractory to steroids and methotrexate. Fusion images (C,D) show excellent co-registration of FDG uptake and MR findings.

in_text_mentions: an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Her diagnosis was established through imaging studies, including aortic CT scan and Doppler ultrasonography, which revealed focal mural calcifications and narrowing of the distal abdominal aorta (Figure 2A, Table 2). Additional findings included diffuse ectasia of the thoracic aorta and stenoses of the renal, iliac, left carotid, and left subclavian arteries. She was treated with prednisone 1 mg/kg/day followed by methotrexate (up to 15 mg/week), achieving clinical and laboratory stability. She has been in remission for at least the past seven years.

in_text_mentions: Our patient experienced characteristic symptoms such as palpitations, headaches, and vision changes for more than 1 month, had moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation and pulmonary artery lesions, thus meeting the modified Ishikawa criteria suggesting high probability of Takayasu arteritis [Table 2]. In addition, surgical pathology demonstrated chronic aortitis with giant cell infiltration consistent with Takayasu arteritis, thus confirming the diagnosis [Figure 2].

c inflammation leads to thickening of the arterial wall, resulting in stenosis and occlusion. In rapid or severe inflammation, the destruction of smooth muscle cells results in weakening of the arterial wall, leading to vascular dilatation and aneurysm formation. The burned-out phase of TAK involves adventitial fibrosis and scarring, along with persistent lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and multinucleated giant cells8. The surgical pathology report for our patient, which showed chronic aortitis with multinucleated giant cell infiltration, is suggestive of the burned-out phase of TAK [Figure 2].

in_text_mentions: halmologic examinations were unremarkable, and there were no signs of joint swelling, cyanosis, pulse differences between upper and lower extremities, or bruits. The patient’s pertinent laboratory workup is displayed in Table 1. An echocardiogram demonstrated an ejection fraction of 59% and a 4.9-cm aortic aneurysm with moderate-to-severe aortic insufficiency. CT angiography (CTA) of the chest showed a 5.0-cm proximal aortic aneurysm [Figure 1]. The patient underwent valve-sparing aortic root and ascending aortic replacement (David-V-Smod procedure) with a 24-mm Terumo Gelweave Valsalva graft.

here are limited reports of TAK with isolated aneurysms in the absence of occlusive lesions6. Our patient’s echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 59% and a 4.9-cm aortic aneurysm with moderate-to-severe aortic insufficiency. CT angiography (CTA) of the chest showed a 5.0-cm proximal aortic aneurysm [Figure 1]. The patient’s CTA of the head and neck did reveal tissue thickening of the walls of the aortic arch and proximal great vessels. However, there was no significant stenosis. Aneurysmal changes are reported mainly in patients older than 40 years, while our patient was 27 years old7.

in_text_mentions: Given the persistent hypertension and clinical suspicion for renovascular pathology, a renal artery duplex ultrasound was performed, which showed elevated peak systolic velocities at the ostium of the left renal artery, suggestive of stenosis. To further evaluate this finding, a CTA of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained. The imaging revealed abnormal, circumferential wall thickening of the infrarenal abdominal aorta, measuring up to 4 mm thick (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: 5.39 mm (Figure 4). Additional imaging showed bilateral occlusion of subclavian arteries from their initial segments. There were extensive collateral branches to intercostal arteries supplying both upper arms (Figures 5 and 6). The terminal aorta was irregular but bilateral renal arteries and other branches of aorta were normal (Figure 7). We started the patient on 20 mg prednisone resulting in a reduction of ESR as well as normalization of C Reactive Protein. Further the patient was referred for endovascular coil embolization as vertebral arteries were relatively straight and easy to access.

in_text_mentions: showed marked isolated short-segment severe stenosis of the aorta between the renal arteries and the IMA. The SMA and IMA were connected through the developed arc of Riolan. There were no findings of blood flow disturbance in the CA or SMA (Fig. 1). Biphasic blood flow below the IMA, direct flow from the aorta, followed by collateral flow via the arc of Riolan and IMA, were observed with diagnostic angiography (Fig. 2). To assess potential relapse of arteritis, additional examinations, including FDG-PET, were conducted and revealed no evidence of active inflammatory uptake in the aortic wall.

in_text_mentions: This finding was radiologically consistent with aortitis, potentially representing early Type IV TA. Additionally, the scan revealed a duplication of the left renal arteries. The anterior left renal artery showed 30% stenosis, while the posterior left renal artery exhibited severe stenosis of approximately 75% (Figure 3). The right renal artery was widely patent. The radiologist noted an overall paucity of atherosclerotic calcifications, further supporting a vasculitic etiology over degenerative disease.

in_text_mentions: Around one month after hospitalization, he developed intermittent upper-limb claudication with a 10 mmHg systolic blood pressure difference between arms (right 145/76 mmHg; left 155/79 mmHg). Based on these findings, a diagnosis of TA was established.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Coronal CT component of PET/CT in Takayasu arteritis case showing thoracic aorta and supra-aortic vessels with inflammatory wall changes corresponding to FDG-avid vasculitis. B: PET coronal image shows circumferential increased FDG uptake in thoracic aorta and supra-aortic branches in titled Takayasu arteritis case, consistent with active large-vessel vasculitis. C: Fused PET/CT shows FDG-avid thoracic aorta, brachiocephalic trunk and carotids, classic active Takayasu large-vessel vasculitis. D: PET MIP shows linear hypermetabolism along aorta and supra-aortic vessels supporting active Takayasu arteritis.
panels.attribution_text: Pereira et al. A Rare Case of Takayasu Arteritis and Aortic Aneurysm in a Male Patient.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.94910. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging. Corresponding CT (A), PET (B), fused PET/CT (C), and PET MIP (D) images showing increased FDG uptake in the thoracic aorta, brachiocephalic trunk, and bilateral carotid arteries, consistent with active large-vessel vasculitis. 18F-FDG, 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose; CT, computed tomography; MIP, maximum intensity projection; PET, positron emission tomography
in_text_mentions: Persistent fever and inflammatory markers prompted an 18F-FDG PET/CT on day 20, showing increased uptake in the thoracic aorta, brachiocephalic trunk, and bilateral carotid and subclavian arteries, consistent with inflammatory involvement (Figure 5).

panels.rationale: Single axial carotid/cerebral CT angiogram from case report titled Atypical Takayasu Arteritis presenting as stroke in young female. Caption directly describes diffusely narrowed right intracranial internal carotid artery in petrous segment, matching smooth tapered arterial stenosis vocabulary. Disease attribution supported by article diagnosis of takayasu_arteritis. Annotated with blue circle.
panels.attribution_text: Gupta et al. Atypical Takayasu Arteritis Presenting as Ischemic Stroke in a Young Female Despite Normal ESR and Preserved Peripheral Pulses: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.114610. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Carotid and cerebral computed tomographic angiography The right internal carotid artery diffusely narrowed (blue circle) in its intracranial course in the petrous segment.
in_text_mentions: internal carotid artery, causing stenosis of approximately 70%. Thick eccentric wall calcification in the supra-clinoid segment and the cavernous segment of the right internal carotid artery (Figure 3), with stenosis of 50% in the petrous segment (Figure 4) and severe stenosis in the supra-clinoid segment (Figure 5), and with complete occlusion in the communicating segment. P1 segment of the right posterior cerebral artery is hypoplastic, and the P2 segment is seen as a continuation og right posterior communicating artery, suggestive of fetal origin of the right posterior communicating artery

Caption and in-text specifically attribute abrupt P1 narrowing with collaterals to this patient, supporting Takayasu-related arterial stenosis. Intracranial PCA involvement is atypical for Takayasu.

There was evidence of abrupt narrowing in the right supraclinoid internal carotid artery (Figure 1) and the P1 segment of the right posterior cerebral artery with multiple collaterals (Figure 2) along the course, replacing them with the right middle cerebral artery, right anterior cerebral artery, and right posterior cerebral artery, likely receiving supply from the opposite side.

panels.rationale: Single CTA patient image from disease-focused Takayasu arteritis case report. Caption describes complete occlusion of communicating right ICA with collateral channels; in-text describes M1 occlusion and reformation via collaterals likely suggestive of vasculitis. Occlusion matches Takayasu branch artery occlusion vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Gupta et al. Atypical Takayasu Arteritis Presenting as Ischemic Stroke in a Young Female Despite Normal ESR and Preserved Peripheral Pulses: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.114610. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 7.
panels.figure_caption: Carotid and cerebral computed tomographic angiography No contrast in the communicating segment of the right internal carotid artery, signifying complex occlusion (blue arrow) with formation of multiple collateral channels (red circle) along the circle of Willis on the right side.
in_text_mentions: municating segment. P1 segment of the right posterior cerebral artery is hypoplastic, and the P2 segment is seen as a continuation og right posterior communicating artery, suggestive of fetal origin of the right posterior communicating artery; however, normal in caliber (Figure 6). Short segment complete occlusion of the M1 segment of the right middle cerebral artery with distal reformation through multiple collateral channels, and reformation of the distal right A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery through the Circle of Willis (Figure 7) and collaterals, likely suggestive of vasculitis.
